failure_modes: Density domination: when the spectrum mostly tracks node or edge count, H_s scales almost perfectly with density and carries little else, so an excellent data collapse can be a trivial one
Comparing spectra of graphs with different Laplacian definitions (combinatorial, normalised, incidence-based)
Eigendecomposition cost on very large graphs
gloss: Entropy of a graph Laplacian's eigenvalues: the diversity of global flow and relaxation modes
invariants: Uses the whole eigenvalue spectrum, so it reflects global rather than local structure
Laplacian eigenvalues are non-negative, so the normalised spectrum is a valid distribution
The zero eigenvalues (one per connected component) contribute nothing
mechanism: Build the graph Laplacian L. For an undirected graph L = D - A, with D the diagonal degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix. For a directed graph use the incidence matrix B (B_ie = +1 if edge e leaves node i, -1 if it enters, 0 otherwise) and L = B B^T. Take its eigenvalues lambda_i, normalise them to p_i = lambda_i / sum_j lambda_j, and compute H_s = -sum_i p_i log2 p_i, the {{shannon_entropy}} of the spectrum. Because the Laplacian governs diffusion, synchronisation and relaxation on the graph, H_s describes global structure: a spread-out spectrum (high H_s) means many distinct flow modes, a concentrated spectrum (low H_s) means regular, modular or tightly structured topology. It complements local measures such as {{degree_entropy}}.
